contributions.text: Consumption beyond the sanctioned load without the Board's consent amounts to theft or malpractice; the statutory tariff (Clause 16.9) empowers the Board to disconnect supply without notice on detecting unauthorised load.

Even if hooking was found, the Board could de-hook, realise the value of unauthorised consumption at the penal rate, or proceed under Section 135 — but that did not authorise the disconnection effected or an illegal assessment.
Section 126 (unauthorised use — civil, no mens rea) and Section 135 (theft — criminal, dishonesty) operate in different fields.

Section 126 assessment may be made even on inspection of records where a person is found in unauthorised use, without attracting Section 135, because Section 135 contemplates a positive act interfering with the recording of electricity supplied.

Sections 126 (civil, no mens rea, unauthorised use of wider purposive connotation covering excess-load/change-of-category under Explanation (b)(iv)) and 135 (criminal, dishonesty) operate in different and distinct fields with no commonality; Sections 126-127 are a complete code, only the final Section 126(3) assessment is appealable under Section 127, and the High Court should not ordinarily interfere with a final assessment under Article 226.

Where a case is treated as theft (FIR lodged, not suspected theft or mere unauthorised use), the Section 126 / Clause 15.7 provisional-assessment machinery and the suspected-theft safeguards of Clause 15.8(x)-(xv) do not apply; the procedure is Section 135(1A)/Clause 15.8(i)-(ix), and mislabelling the theft bill as a Section 126 assessment does not convert the proceeding.

Section 126 (civil assessment) and Sections 135–140 (criminal offences) apply in parallel to the same act of unauthorised use; a Section 126 assessment is a civil/quasi-judicial consequence, not a criminal adjudication.

An assessment under Section 126 must be made even where a Section 135 theft offence has been booked and is pending before the Special Court; the Special Court's civil-liability determination under Section 154(5) does not oust the assessing officer's Section 126 power. The two tracks (civil assessment + criminal trial) run in parallel.

Sections 126 and 135 operate in different and distinct fields; theft under Section 135 cannot be assessed under Section 126, and its civil liability is measured under the Section 154(5) formula, subject to final adjudication by the Special Court.

Section 135 theft falls within criminal jurisprudence and mens rea is the relevant factor; Section 126 (read with the Supply Code) does not speak of criminal intent, and the assessment under it is appealable under Section 127, whereas a Section 135 assessment (Reg. 23-AA) has no statutory appeal.

A Section 126 assessment may be made even in theft cases and is unaffected by the outcome of the Section 135 prosecution — an acquittal (a fortiori a benefit-of-doubt acquittal) does not exonerate the civil liability under Section 126; Section 154(5) does not oust Section 126, and an un-appealed final assessment attains finality.

Theft under Section 135 is a subset of 'unauthorised use', so a Section 126 assessment may be made even in theft cases; the Section 126(1) assessment and the Section 154(5) Special Court determination are not parallel/mutually exclusive and may both proceed, the Section 126 assessment requiring only civil proof (preponderance), not proof beyond reasonable doubt.

Because unauthorised use (Section 126) is the genus and theft (Section 135) a species, a Section 126 assessment must be made even in theft cases (with a Section 127 appeal); an FIR/final report under Section 135 does not bar it, and the Special Court finally determines civil liability under Section 154(6).

Even where an FIR is lodged under Section 135, the assessment is carried out under Section 126 (with the Section 127 appeal remedy), and the Special Court finally determines the civil liability under Section 154(6).

Because unauthorised use (Section 126, civil, preponderance of probability) is the genus and theft (Section 135, criminal, proof beyond reasonable doubt + mens rea) only a species, an acquittal on a theft charge does not ipso facto extinguish civil liability under Section 126; the two channels operate on separate footings.

Although Sections 126 and 135 run in parallel with different proof standards, where the Section 126 assessment rests solely on the self-same allegation (tampered/bypassed meter) as the Section 135 prosecution, an honourable acquittal exonerates the consumer under Section 126 too, because the same charge cannot survive on preponderance of probability once it has failed beyond reasonable doubt.
An acquittal in the Section 135 criminal case does not exonerate Section 126 civil liability (the two proceedings have no bearing on each other).

Sections 126 and 135 are constitutionally valid: their overlap on tampering permits parallel Section 126 assessment and Section 135 Special-Court trial without double standards; no hearing is due before a non-conclusive provisional assessment; the assessing officer is an independent State appointee; and the Section 127(2) 50% pre-deposit is valid and beyond Article 226 interference.

contributions.text: The Section 127 appellate authority must apply its own mind, read the relevant provisions and pass a reasoned, speaking order; a shallow, non-speaking affirmance cannot stand.

Sections 126 and 127 read together constitute a complete code; only a final order of assessment under Section 126(3) is appealable under Section 127, and a notice-cum-provisional assessment under Section 126(2) is not appealable.

The High Court should normally decline to interfere under Article 226 with a final assessment; it may examine a jurisdictional challenge but must not travel into the assessing officer's exclusive domain of assessment and fact-finding.

A Section 127 appeal lies only against a Section 126 order; a Section 135(1A)/theft assessment is not appealable under Section 127 and is examinable only by the Special Court under Section 154(5)/(6).
The remedy against a final Section 126 order is an appeal to the appellate authority under Section 127, entertained only on deposit of half the assessed amount; the appellate order is final.

A Section 126 final assessment in a theft case is appealable under Section 127 (following Paliwal Alloys); a writ was nonetheless entertained here because jurisdiction was challenged and the order breached natural justice.

The limitation for a Section 127 appeal against a Section 126 assessment is subject to Section 14 of the Limitation Act (Electricity Act being a special law under Section 29(2)): time spent bona fide pursuing a writ remedy in the wrong forum is excluded, so the appeal is not time-barred; Section 125 (SC appeal from the Appellate Tribunal) is distinct and its limitation authority does not apply.

Even a consumer who has compounded and paid the compounding fee should be permitted to test the correctness of the manner of computation of the civil liability fastened on him; there is a casus omissus (no forum to test the final Section 135 assessment).
An appellate order rejecting a Section 127 appeal as not maintainable, passed without affording any opportunity of hearing, warrants interference and is quashed and remitted.
Where no Section 127 appeal is filed against the final Section 126 assessment, it attains finality and the consumer is liable to pay the assessed amount.

A Section 126 assessment is to be made even where an offence under Section 135 has been made out (FIR/final report notwithstanding); the Special Court finally determines the civil liability, with further action under Section 154(6).

On a Section 127 appeal remanded solely on quantum, the Appellate Authority is bound by the finding that Section 126 applies and cannot re-litigate applicability; its remit is confined to the quantum of assessment.

A Section 126 assessment is appealable under Section 127 to the notified appellate authority (in U.P., the Commissioner of the Division) even when an FIR under Section 135 exists; the appellate authority cannot decline jurisdiction, and the Special Court finally determines civil liability under Section 154(6).

A consumer who forgoes the Section 127 appeal (and its 50% pre-deposit) and lets the assessment attain finality cannot secure unqualified restoration of supply via a writ; Section 145 bars civil-court interference with Section 126/127 assessments.
No Section 127 appeal lay because no final order of assessment was ever made; hence the writ under Article 226 is maintainable.
A consumer who lets the Section 127 appeal become time-barred cannot, absent palpable arbitrariness, obtain relief by a direct writ under Article 226.

contributions.text: A Section 126 provisional assessment must (a) be made under Section 126 itself, not under the Board's old supply conditions, and (b) be the assessing officer's own best judgment on his personal observation; an assessment dictated by a superior's guideline is a nullity, and coerced payment on an illegal assessment is recoverable as unjust enrichment.

It was noted (relying on the Board's contention and Mam Chand) that Section 145 of the 2003 Act expressly bars the civil court from entertaining suits on matters falling under Section 126, the Act being a complete code, so assessment disputes should go to the competent authority under the Act.

Assessment of the charge for unauthorised use, meter-tampering and calibration are technical matters; whether the beneficial consumer jurisdiction extends to such determinations (and to tortious acts like disconnection) is left open and remitted to the National Commission.

An assessing officer cannot make a theft assessment without first establishing a case of theft (para 8.1(b)(iv)); the best-judgment assessment must be reasoned, unbiased and rational, an oral hearing must be given, and theft cannot be inferred on mere presumption or on readings of meters not installed at the consumer's premises absent a specific enabling provision.
'Unauthorised use of electricity' under Section 126 deals with cases of unauthorised use even in the absence of intention — distinct from dishonest abstraction under Section 135.

'Unauthorised use of electricity' is an expression of wider connotation to be construed purposively; excess-load consumption beyond the connected load falls under Explanation (b)(iv) to Section 126 (besides violating the Regulations and agreement).

A final assessment under Section 126 for 'unauthorised use of electricity' is a quasi-judicial decision by a public servant; it is not a 'consumer dispute' under Section 2(1)(e) of the Consumer Protection Act, 1986, and cannot be challenged by a consumer complaint.

'Unauthorised use of electricity' (s.126) is the genus of which the theft acts in s.135(1) are species; theft is unauthorised use done dishonestly. A Section 126 assessment therefore has to follow in every case of unauthorised use, including theft — neither section excludes the other.

Under Section 126(6) 'twice the tariff' ordinarily embraces both fixed and energy charges, and higher-tariff misuse is assessed at twice the higher tariff; but where the sole irregularity is excess load in the same premises for the same purpose (no tariff change) and the energy is already metered and paid, the penalty is confined to twice the fixed charges, absent a need to upgrade the distribution system/voltage.
Section 126 assessment is intention-neutral (no mens rea); the assessing officer's presence at inspection is not a mandatory precondition to initiating proceedings.

The condition precedent to a provisional assessment under Section 126(1) is a conclusion by the Assessing Officer that the person is indulging in unauthorised use; that satisfaction cannot rest on the officer's mere 'vagaries' without a fair opportunity of hearing in defence.

A Section 126 inspection alleging unauthorised use should be conducted in the consumer's presence; and the Section 126(5) 12-month cap applies only where the period of unauthorised use is unascertainable.
The authorities are empowered to make a provisional and final assessment under Section 126(1) even in cases where electricity is unauthorisedly used by way of theft.

Consuming electricity beyond the sanctioned contract demand, resulting in a change of tariff category, is unauthorised use under Explanation (b)(iv) to Section 126 (Seetaram Rice Mill); the assessment follows Sections 126(3)-(6), and prior payment of a contract-demand penalty is no bar to it.

Raising a short-assessment demand to correct the licensee's own wrong multiply-factor is not a 'deficiency in service' where the consumer does not dispute the short-billing; it is 'escaped assessment', so the consumer fora cannot interfere.

The provisional assessment must be supplied to the consumer under Section 126(2); in the absence of such service there should be no demand, because a statutory power must be exercised only in the manner prescribed and not otherwise.

A decision under Section 126 must be taken strictly in accordance with the statutory provision — when a statute provides that a thing be done in a particular manner, it must be done in that manner and not in any other.

The assessing officer is a State Government appointee (whether of the Government or the licensee) and so has an independent character, not functioning merely as an employee of the licensee — hence no unbridled power and no basis to strike down the Section.

contributions.text: Corroboration of suspected unauthorised use / DAE by the consumer's consumption pattern (Reg. 26(ii)) is a precondition to the exercise of the assessing officer's jurisdiction; if consumption exceeds the prescribed threshold, no case can be booked.

The assessing officer has no jurisdiction to make a theft assessment unless he first establishes a case of theft against the person (para 8.1(b)(iv)); merely issuing a provisional assessment order does not establish theft.
Theft of electrical energy cannot be made out on mere presumption; it has to be established as required by para 8.1(b)(iv) of the Code.

A missing/tampered seal or broken glass window is not, by itself, evidence of theft unless corroborated by the consumer's consumption pattern and other available evidence — this is the safeguard for suspected-theft cases (Clause 15.8(x)-(xv)).
To prove theft in a criminal proceeding, the case must be proved beyond reasonable doubt with mens rea established; such strict proof is not necessary for assessing liability under Section 126(1).

A Section 126 assessment is a civil enquiry to be decided on the standard of preponderance of probability, whereas Section 135 theft requires proof beyond reasonable doubt with mens rea; the yardsticks are distinct.

Sections 126 and 135 operate in separate fields and parallel proceedings may run; Section 126 is civil (preponderance of probability), Section 135 is criminal (beyond reasonable doubt) — the standards of proof differ.

Where a tampered/bypassed meter is the ONLY allegation and it founds both the Section 135 prosecution and the Section 126 assessment (self-same allegation), an acquittal scot-free in the criminal case means the consumer cannot be indicted for the same charge even on a preponderance of probability.

contributions.text: A Section 152 compounding is a deemed acquittal that bars the Special Court from thereafter determining civil liability under Section 154(5) (civil liability being predicated on a positive determination of the offence); and compounding under Section 152 cannot be effected without the complainant-licensee's consent.
Compounding under Section 152 is available both for established and for suspected theft; it is offered before the consumer is proceeded against before the Special Court.

Compounding under Section 152 is an admission of guilt (deemed acquittal) and cannot be made under protest; the consumer who compounds cannot reopen the finding of guilt, but he may test the manner of computation of the civil liability, and an appeal cannot be rejected without a hearing.

contributions.scope: SC-binding (on the CPA 'service' point); the Section 145 bar recorded, not finally adjudicated
contributions.text: Electricity supply is a 'service' under the Consumer Protection Act, but assessment disputes under Section 126 engage the Section 145 civil-court bar and the complete-code character of the 2003 Act; whether the consumer fora's jurisdiction extends to such technical/assessment disputes is left open and remitted.

In an electricity-theft case, the civil court's jurisdiction to entertain a suit challenging the theft bill / civil liability is impliedly ousted by Sections 153–154 (Special Court), even where no criminal complaint is filed; Section 145's express bar is confined to Section 126/127 assessment matters. The plaint was rightly rejected, though for different reasons than the Single Judge gave.

The High Court should normally decline to interfere under Article 226 with a final assessment; it may examine a jurisdictional challenge but must not travel into the assessing officer's exclusive domain of assessment and fact-finding.
The Section 127 appeal lies only against a Section 126 order, not against a Section 135(1A)/Clause 15.8 theft assessment; the latter is examinable by the Special Court under Section 154(5)/(6).
The remedy against a final theft assessment is before the Special Court under Section 154(5)/(6), which determines the civil liability; the writ court will not interfere.

A consumer complaint challenging a Section 126 assessment or any Sections 135–140 action is not maintainable before a Consumer Forum; the statutory remedies (Section 127 appeal; Special Court under Section 153) are exclusive of the consumer route.

Section 145 excludes the civil court's jurisdiction over matters an assessing officer (Section 126) or appellate authority (Section 127) is empowered to determine; a court entertaining an unauthorised-abstraction suit must decide that jurisdictional bar first, and the licensee may raise it as respondent without a cross-appeal.
Theft of electricity under Section 135 (punishable up to three years) is a cognizable offence; the CrPC therefore applies and it is the duty of the police to register an FIR and investigate.

Section 151 enables authorised persons to file a written complaint before the Court (on which cognizance may be taken straightway), but it does not exclude the other avenue of a police FIR/investigation; the Electricity Act is not a complete machinery for how offences are dealt with, so the CrPC governs.

The amendment (proviso) to Section 151 permitting cognizance on a police report is clarificatory in nature and applies to pending matters (retrospective); notwithstanding Section 151, an FIR could be filed with the police even under the unamended provision.
The contrary High Court view (complaint-only route) does not lay down correct law; the police-FIR-competent view is approved — resolving the split.

The Special Court's power under Section 154(5) to determine civil liability for theft does not preclude a Section 126 assessment; the amount 'deposited' referred to in Section 154(6) is the amount assessed under Section 126, there being no other provision for such a deposit.

Civil liability under Section 154(5) is defined (Explanation) as loss 'due to the commission of an offence', so its determination must necessarily be preceded by a positive determination of the commission of the offence.

After a deemed acquittal by compounding under Section 152(3), the Special Court cannot determine civil liability under Section 154(5); there is no different consequence between an acquittal after full trial and a deemed acquittal by compounding.

The Special Court combines both criminal and civil jurisdictions, so the view that a criminal court cannot determine civil liability is incorrect; but its conclusion that no civil liability can be determined after a compounding-acquittal is correct.

Section 126 cannot be applied to assess the amount to be charged for theft of electricity; the civil liability for theft is measured under the Section 154(5) formula (twice the tariff for the twelve months preceding detection, or the exact period of theft if determined, whichever is less), subject to final adjudication by the Special Court.

The amount 'deposited by the consumer' in Section 154(6) is the amount deposited under Section 126 (there being no other deposit provision for theft), so the Section 154(5) Special Court does not oust the Section 126 assessment; the argument that only the Special Court may assess is rejected.

The Section 126(1) assessment power and the Section 154(5) Special Court power to determine civil liability are not parallel to each other; the High Court erred in holding that both proceedings cannot operate parallelly.

Where there is no theft (only unauthorised use), no Section 135 complaint lies and the loss is assessed under Section 126(1); where the unauthorised use amounts to theft, a Section 126(1) assessment AND a Section 135 complaint may both proceed, with the Special Court determining civil liability under Section 154(5) and any excess deposit refunded.

Merely because the Special Court is empowered to determine civil liability under Section 154(5) where a complaint is lodged, it cannot be said that the authorities have no power to make a Section 126 assessment.

The 'amount deposited by the consumer' in Section 154(6) is the amount deposited under Section 126 — there being no other deposit provision for theft — so Section 126 assessment and the Special Court's Section 154(5) determination coexist.

Raising a short-assessment demand to correct the licensee's own wrong multiply-factor is not a 'deficiency in service' where the consumer does not dispute the short-billing; it is 'escaped assessment', so the consumer fora cannot interfere.
A consumer forum must, at the threshold, find whether there was any deficiency in service before it can test the licensee's recovery against Section 56.

Section 145 bars civil-court interference in respect of assessments under Sections 126 and 127; a Section 135 FIR instead leads to a Section 154 Special Court criminal action, with civil liability under Section 154(5) independent of and subject to the Section 126 deposit (Section 154(6)).

The Explanation to Section 154(6) ('civil liability') refers to the liability determined by the Special Court under Section 154(5) for theft, not to the amount raised as a provisional assessment under Section 126.

Electricity arrears of a previous owner/occupier are recoverable from a transferee/auction-purchaser as a precondition to supply where a statutory Condition of Supply / Supply Code so provides; the Section 43 duty to supply is not absolute, the Sections 50/181 (and 1948 Act Section 49) powers can create a statutory charge on the premises, and the suit remedy is independent of the Section 56 disconnection remedy.

contributions.text: For Section 56(2), a Section 126 electricity due becomes 'first due' only on the making of the final assessment; the two-year recovery bar runs from that date, not from detection or consumption.

Charges become 'first due' under Section 56(2) only on issuance of the bill; the Section 56(1) disconnection right is subject to a two-year limitation from that date; beyond two years the licensee may raise a supplementary demand and pursue other recovery modes (limitation for a suit on a mistake running from discovery under Section 17(1)(c) Limitation Act) but cannot disconnect supply.

contributions.scope: SC-binding (2-Judge; distinguishes the 3-Judge Rahamatullah Khan on facts)
contributions.text: Section 56(2) bars both recovery and disconnection (its disconnection bar being an exception to the ordinary law of limitation), but the bar is keyed to a consumer's neglect to pay a 'sum due'; a licensee's correction of its own short-billing mistake is escaped assessment (not deficiency in service and not a consumer's default), and limitation runs only from when a bill/demand is raised.
The power to initiate recovery proceedings by filing a suit against a defaulting consumer is independent of the power to disconnect supply as a means of recovery under Section 56.

line_of_authority.title: Md. Abdul Matin v. West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd.

contributions.text: Section 126 assessment may be made even on inspection of records where a person is found in unauthorised use, without attracting Section 135, because Section 135 contemplates a positive act interfering with the recording of electricity supplied.

Section 135 theft falls within criminal jurisprudence and mens rea is a relevant factor; Section 126 does not speak of any criminal intendment and is primarily a civil remedy without elements traceable to mens rea.
'Unauthorised use of electricity' under Section 126 deals with cases of unauthorised use even in the absence of intention — distinct from dishonest abstraction under Section 135.

Sections 126 and 135 sit in different Parts (XII vs XIV), cover different fields and prescribe different procedures; theft involves mens rea, which is not necessary for unauthorised use under Section 126.

Offences under Sections 135–140 (theft and allied acts) are triable only by a Special Court constituted under Section 153; a Consumer Forum has no jurisdiction over any action taken under Sections 135–140.

Theft of electricity under Section 135 is a cognizable offence governed by the CrPC; the police may register an FIR, investigate and file a Section 173 report on which the Court takes cognizance, and the Section 151 complaint route does not exclude this — the 2007 proviso to Section 151 being clarificatory and retrospective.

A show-cause notice / opportunity of hearing is required only where theft is suspected (broken/tampered seals, no evidence at site — per Circular 54/2007); where the theft is 'writ large' (here a dead-stop meter with a soldered wire after breaking the counter lock), no opportunity of hearing need be given before proceeding.

'Unauthorised use of electricity' under Section 126 covers cases of unauthorised use even without intention; the consumer's intention is not the foundation for an assessment order under Section 126 (mens rea is a Section 135 concept).

Section 135 theft falls within criminal jurisprudence and mens rea is the relevant factor; Section 126 (read with the Supply Code) does not speak of criminal intent, and the assessment under it is appealable under Section 127, whereas a Section 135 assessment (Reg. 23-AA) has no statutory appeal.

A Section 135 criminal proceeding has no bearing on a Section 126 proceeding; even an acquittal in the criminal case for a Section 135 offence does not exonerate the consumer from Section 126 civil liability.

On the facts, the acquittal was not a clean acquittal but a benefit-of-doubt acquittal on technicality (delayed seizure, non-production of dump copy), reinforcing that it does not undo the Section 126 civil liability.
To prove theft in a criminal proceeding, the case must be proved beyond reasonable doubt with mens rea established; such strict proof is not necessary for assessing liability under Section 126(1).

Unauthorised use of electricity (Explanation (b) to Section 126) is the genus of which the Section 135(1) acts are species; theft is unauthorised use done dishonestly, so a Section 126 assessment must follow whenever there is unauthorised use.

Following Seetaram Rice Mill (para 35), intention is not the foundation for invoking Section 126; all that need be ascertained is whether the consumer exceeded the contract load resulting in usage beyond it.

An acquittal on a Section 135 theft charge (tested on proof beyond reasonable doubt) does not ipso facto exonerate the consumer from civil liability under Section 126 (tested on the more liberal preponderance of probability).

Where a tampered/bypassed meter is the ONLY allegation and it founds both the Section 135 prosecution and the Section 126 assessment (self-same allegation), an acquittal scot-free in the criminal case means the consumer cannot be indicted for the same charge even on a preponderance of probability.

The contention that an acquittal in the Section 135 criminal case extinguishes Section 126 liability is not acceptable — a Section 135 proceeding has no bearing on a Section 126 proceeding (following Orion Metal and Seetaram Rice Mill).

A Section 126 finding does not indict a person of theft (a criminal charge); the assessing officer merely calculates the licensee's loss, and whether theft is established is left to the Special Court's full criminal trial — so no violation of Articles 19/21.

line_of_authority.title: Md. Abdul Matin v. West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd.

contributions.text: Under a statutory tariff clause, disconnection of supply on detecting excess-load/theft may be effected without prior notice (natural justice yielding to the urgency of protecting the Board's property), but the ensuing assessment of the value of energy and compensation must be made only after a hearing.

Section 126(1) requires the assessing officer to provisionally assess 'to the best of his judgment' on his own personal observation of the extent of unauthorised use; this quasi-judicial function cannot be fettered by a superior's guideline/office order — an assessment dictated by such a direction is the direction-giver's judgment, not the officer's, and is illegal.

In a Section 126 unauthorised-use / DAE proceeding the show-cause notice must precisely disclose the grounds — including the consumption-pattern basis relied on — and the licensee must grant a real hearing; a demand founded on seal/glass irregularities without that disclosure or corroboration is set aside and remitted.
The law requires an opportunity of oral hearing to the consumer before final assessment; none was given here (no date was communicated for the consumer to answer the charges in person).

A missing/tampered seal or broken glass window is not, by itself, evidence of theft unless corroborated by the consumer's consumption pattern and other available evidence — this is the safeguard for suspected-theft cases (Clause 15.8(x)-(xv)).

A final assessment under Section 126 passed beyond the 30-day window in Section 126(3) — here two years after the provisional notice and without a fresh hearing — is void for breach of natural justice and is set aside with a direction to reassess after hearing objections.

A pre-assessment hearing in a theft case is required only where theft is merely suspected; where theft is 'writ large' on the checking report, no opportunity of hearing need be afforded before the licensee proceeds.
The physical presence of the assessing officer at the time of inspection and detection of unauthorised use is not a mandatory precondition for initiating assessment proceedings under Section 126(1).

A Section 126 assessment is subject to natural justice: the provisional assessment presupposes a lawful conclusion of unauthorised use, and a final assessment (or any coerced deposit) is invalid unless the consumer's objections are considered and a personal hearing given, per Section 126(3) and Clause 8.1 of the 2005 Supply Code.

An inspection alleging unauthorised use under Section 126 should be conducted in the presence of the consumer (a signatory to the inspection report); the licensee's failure to show the night inspection was in the consumer's presence undermined its case.
An appellate order rejecting a Section 127 appeal as not maintainable, passed without affording any opportunity of hearing, warrants interference and is quashed and remitted.
It is the incumbent duty of the licensee to pass a final order of assessment within 30 days of service of the provisional assessment, even if the consumer files no objection.

The Section 126(2)/(3) procedure — service of the provisional assessment, opportunity to object, and a final assessment — is mandatory (manner-prescribed rule); a demand raised without it is set aside and remitted.

No hearing is required before a provisional assessment under Section 126(1) (which is not conclusive); the right of hearing and to file objections is given before the final order, and requiring a hearing before the provisional assessment would defeat the summary, expeditious timeline.

contributions.text: Although natural justice is excluded at the disconnection stage, the determination of the value of energy consumed and the assessment of compensation must be made after giving the affected person an opportunity of hearing — that requirement is read into the clause even though it is silent.

Sections 126 and 127 read together constitute a complete code; only a final order of assessment under Section 126(3) is appealable under Section 127, and a notice-cum-provisional assessment under Section 126(2) is not appealable.

The suspected-theft safeguards in Clause 15.8(x)-(xv) (continued supply, provisional assessment, show-cause, 75%-consumption drop) have no application to a clear theft case, which is governed by Clause 15.8(i)-(ix).

Labelling a theft demand as a 'Section 126 provisional assessment' does not convert a theft proceeding into a Section 126 assessment where, on the date of inspection, it was treated as theft (FIR lodged) and not even as suspected theft.

A final assessment must be passed within thirty days of the provisional order under Section 126(3); a final order passed about two years later, without a fresh opportunity of hearing, violates natural justice and cannot be sustained.

A final assessment made without considering the consumer's objections and without a personal hearing (as required by Section 126(3) and Clause 8.1(b)(iii) of the 2005 Code) is dehors the statutory provision and cannot stand.
Absent a lawful final assessment made after considering objections and hearing, the consumer cannot be compelled to deposit the provisional amount.
Where no Section 127 appeal is filed against the final Section 126 assessment, it attains finality and the consumer is liable to pay the assessed amount.

The U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 (Clause 8.1) requires a provisional assessment bill and final assessment even in Section 135 theft cases, confirming that assessment for theft is made under Section 126.

A consumer who bypasses the Section 127 appeal (which requires a 50% pre-deposit) cannot obtain from the writ court, indirectly, the restoration he could not get from the appellate forum; there is no unqualified restoration without complying with the final assessment.

The licensee has a duty to pass a final Section 126 assessment within 30 days of serving the provisional order (even absent objection); failing that, the provisional order spends its force after 30 days and any amount paid on it is refundable.

The provisional assessment must be supplied to the consumer under Section 126(2); in the absence of such service there should be no demand, because a statutory power must be exercised only in the manner prescribed and not otherwise.
A demand issued without considering the consumer's objection and without making a final assessment requires interference and must be remitted for a fresh decision strictly per Section 126.

No hearing is required before a provisional assessment under Section 126(1) (which is not conclusive); the right of hearing and to file objections is given before the final order, and requiring a hearing before the provisional assessment would defeat the summary, expeditious timeline.
